canonical_topic: Formation and trapping of natural gas
definition: Natural gas forms from decaying organic material and becomes economically recoverable only when an impermeable rock layer prevents the resulting methane from escaping to the surface.
core_idea: Methane is a common byproduct of decomposing organic matter; it normally disperses into the atmosphere, but when trapped beneath impermeable rock it accumulates underground, dispersed through small connected pores rather than pooling in an open cavern.
key_points: Natural gas is often found dissolved in oil fields, coal beds, and underground rock formations.
Underground deposits can be millions of years old, but methane can also form quickly from modern decomposing waste (e.g., landfills).
Trapped gas typically resides dispersed in small holes of a porous rock layer, not in a large open cavity.
Exploration targets a permeable rock layer sitting beneath an impermeable cap layer, since gas must be able to flow toward a well to be extracted.
caveats: That underground gas deposits are large open caves rather than gas dispersed through porous rock.
